clinicalPearls: A chronic condition of persistent pelvic or bladder pain, pressure, or discomfort perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency, in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause
It is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring symptoms to be present for a sustained period (typically several weeks) with negative cultures and exclusion of confusable diseases
Predominantly affects women and is frequently associated with other chronic pain and functional disorders such as fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and chronic fatigue
Cystoscopy with hydrodistension may reveal Hunner lesions (inflamed mucosal patches) in a minority, defining a distinct ulcerative phenotype, or glomerulations, which are non-specific
Pain characteristically worsens with bladder filling and is relieved, at least transiently, by voiding
Symptoms often fluctuate with flares, and certain foods, stress, or menstruation may act as triggers

Management is multimodal and stepwise, including patient education, dietary and behavioural measures, physical therapy for pelvic floor dysfunction, oral and intravesical treatments, and, for refractory Hunner lesions, targeted endoscopic therapy, with major surgery a last resort
reference.pathophysiology: The cause of interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome is not fully understood and is probably multifactorial. A leading hypothesis is that a defective urothelial glycosaminoglycan (GAG) mucous layer allows urinary solutes such as potassium to penetrate the bladder wall, provoking sensory nerve activation, mast cell recruitment, and neurogenic inflammation. Chronic activation leads to central and peripheral sensitisation, upregulated bladder afferents, and, in some patients, mucosal inflammation with Hunner lesions. Overlap with other chronic pain syndromes suggests that abnormal pain processing and visceral hypersensitivity contribute substantially, so the bladder may be one manifestation of a wider sensory disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent bacterial cystitis or other urinary tract infection
Carcinoma in situ of the bladder
Endometriosis and other gynaecological pelvic pain
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome / prostatitis in men
Bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic bladder
Urethral diverticulum or pelvic floor dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and culture to exclude infection
Urine cytology and cystoscopy to exclude malignancy, particularly carcinoma in situ
Cystoscopy with hydrodistension to identify Hunner lesions or glomerulations
Symptom and pain questionnaires and a voiding diary to characterise severity
Pelvic examination and assessment of pelvic floor muscle tenderness
Gynaecological evaluation and imaging where pelvic pathology is suspected
redFlags: Macroscopic haematuria or abnormal cytology suggesting bladder malignancy
Persistent sterile pyuria warranting exclusion of tuberculosis or carcinoma in situ
New neurological symptoms or a suspected neurogenic bladder
Escalating opioid use and worsening disability
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and often relapsing rather than curable; many patients achieve meaningful symptom control with a stepwise multimodal approach, though the Hunner-lesion phenotype behaves differently and a minority with refractory disease may ultimately require major reconstructive or ablative surgery.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the syndrome without excluding infection, carcinoma in situ, and gynaecological causes
Treating repeatedly for presumed infection despite negative cultures
Overlooking pelvic floor dysfunction, which is a key and treatable contributor
Escalating to irreversible surgery before exhausting conservative and intravesical options
references: European Association of Urology Guidelines on Chronic Pelvic Pain
